analysis.one_liner: Strengthens enforcement of the rule that insurers cover mental health care on equal terms with medical care.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in July 2022 with 14 Senate sponsors, all Democrats or independents, and died in the Senate Health Committee without a hearing, a vote, or any floor action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law already requires health plans to cover mental health and addiction treatment on par with physical health care, but enforcement has been weak. This bill would force insurers and the companies that administer their plans to submit their parity compliance analyses every year, submit to random federal audits of at least 40 plans per year, publicly disclose how often they deny mental health claims and how little they pay mental health providers compared to medical providers, and respond to consumer complaints through a new federal hotline and website. It would also fund state consumer assistance offices that help people appeal denied mental health claims.
analysis.who_benefits: People with mental health or substance use disorders whose insurance plans deny or shortchange their care, the family members and providers who help them fight those denials, and states that would get grants to run consumer assistance offices helping people file appeals.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People denied mental health and addiction care

how_it_helps.text: Requires insurers to submit their mental health parity compliance analyses annually and on regulator request, and expands the number of plans reviewed each year from at least 20 to at least 60 [S3].
Directs federal agencies to conduct randomized audits of at least 40 health plans per year for parity compliance, plus audits of any plan named in a consumer complaint [S3].

Requires annual public reports comparing denial rates, network adequacy, wait times, and reimbursement rates for mental health services versus medical services, broken down by inpatient, outpatient, emergency, and prescription drug claims [S3].

Creates a federal consumer parity unit with a toll-free number and public website portal for filing parity complaints, requires plans to answer complaints within 7 days and agencies to respond to consumers within 90 days, and publicly names plans that fail audits [S3].

Appropriates $30 million for the federal enforcement unit and $25 million in grants to state consumer assistance and ombudsman offices that help people file mental health claim appeals and enroll in coverage [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and third-party plan administrators bear the audit, disclosure, and complaint-response costs, which they could pass into premiums; federal taxpayers fund the $55 million in first-year appropriations, and group health plan sponsors face new compliance paperwork [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers, plan administrators, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The audit, reporting, and 7-day complaint-response requirements add substantial compliance costs for insurers and the employers who sponsor health plans, costs that tend to show up in premiums [S3].
The bill appropriates $55 million for its first year and leaves later years funded at 'such sums as may be necessary,' an open-ended federal commitment with no cost cap [S3].

Publicly naming and shaming plans over incomplete or unfavorable parity analyses applies the same reporting burden to plans regardless of whether their disparities reflect bad intent or genuine shortages of mental health providers in their networks [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is an enforcement and transparency measure, not a new entitlement: it does not expand what must be covered, it pressures insurers to actually follow rules already on the books. The main real costs are compliance paperwork and $55 million in first-year federal spending, which are modest next to the sums consumers lose when mental health claims are denied at higher rates or reimbursed far below medical claims. A fair-minded reader could object that the public-naming provisions are blunt, but the core design is sound.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late July 2022, referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, and sat there with no hearing, markup, or floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2023 [S5].

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on July 26, 2022, joined by 13 cosponsors: 12 Senate Democrats and 1 independent [S4].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S1].
That referral was the last action of any kind on the bill; no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action ever occurred before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and the third-party administrators that run their plans, who avoid the annual audits, public disparity reports, and complaint-response requirements; the $55 million in enforcement and consumer-assistance funding was never spent. Consumers fighting mental health claim denials gained nothing.

for.name: Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, which strengthened federal enforcement of mental health parity requirements through audits, public disparity reporting, and a consumer complaint unit.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor of the bill, the only non-Democrat among the 14 sponsors.

against.name: Patty Murray
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee where the bill was referred, never brought it to a hearing, markup, or vote; it sat without action from its July 2022 referral until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 14 sponsors were Democrats or independents and no Republican sponsored it; no vote ever took place, so the partisan split in the record is entirely on the sponsorship side [S4].

industries.note: The bill targets exactly the practices insurers profit from: denying mental health claims more often than medical claims and reimbursing mental health providers less, which the bill would force into annual public reporting. It also subjects them to random audits and public naming for incomplete parity analyses, making enforcement of rules already on the books real instead of nominal.

The bill expressly extends every requirement — annual parity analyses, audits, complaint response, and public reporting — to third-party administrators, who currently sit outside the direct line of enforcement. Their business depends on administering plans cost-effectively, and the bill adds audit exposure and disclosure duties.

industries.industry: Mental health and substance use treatment providers
industries.note: Public reporting of reimbursement rates and network wait times, backed by audits, pressures insurers to pay behavioral health providers at rates closer to medical services and to build real networks. Providers benefit directly, and so do their patients.
